reading.rtitle: Twice a Week Is a Habit
paras: Ask anybody how often they exercise, and you will usually hear the same answer: three times a week. Ask them what they did last week, and the real number is often closer to once. They are not lying. They are describing the week they plan to have, not the week they actually have.

A family therapist in Miami says this happens with almost every habit. Parents say they always read with their children at night. In fact, most of them read together two or three times a week, and on the busy days somebody skips it. That is not a failure. Something that happens twice a week, on a regular basis, is still a habit. The problem starts when we say always, feel bad about the days we miss, and then stop completely.

Her advice is simple. First, be honest about the number: never say always if it is only sometimes. Second, choose a frequency you can stick to. Once a week for a year is better than every day for a month. Third, squeeze the small things into moments that already exist. A short chore, like answering messages, fits into the ten minutes before dinner. A longer one needs its own place in the week, and you have to make time for it.

The fourth piece of advice is the one people forget. Keep something that is only a treat: a novel you read now and then, a coffee with a friend every other Saturday, a long bath when everybody is asleep. Busy people hardly ever skip their duties. They skip the things that help them unwind, and those are the things that make the rest of the week possible.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from a conversation with a family therapist about routines.

choices: To prove that most people lie about how often they exercise, read with their children and do the things they promise.
To say that a habit does not need to be daily, and how to choose one you can keep.
To tell busy parents that they should read with their children every single night of the week.

items.situation: A new friend at the club asks: how often do you come here?
tips: I come every Tuesday, after school, with my daughters.
Every plus a day: every Tuesday, every morning.

Once, twice, then three times: never two times for week.

items.situation: Say one thing you always do at the practice, and one thing you never do.
tips: I always check the schedule before eight, and I never answer my phone with a patient in the chair.
The adverb goes before the main verb: I always check.

items.situation: Say how often you are tired on a Tuesday night.

With be, the adverb goes after it: I am usually tired.

Now and then usually goes at the start or the end of the sentence.

items.situation: Ask the patient in your chair about one of his habits.
tips: How often plus do or does: never how much often.

listenings.text: I have cleaned teeth for fifteen years, and there is one question I ask every patient: how often do you floss? Almost everybody says every day. About one in ten actually does. I know, because the gums always tell the truth. So these days I ask the question differently. I say: when did you last floss? That question gets an honest answer, because it asks about one day, not about a habit. And the honest answer is usually useful. Most people floss two or three times a week, normally in the evening, and hardly ever in the morning, because mornings are a rush. My advice is not to promise every day. Floss once a day, at the same time, right after something you never skip, like brushing your teeth at night. A small habit attached to a big one almost always survives. A small habit on its own almost never does.

We have two kids and two jobs, so our week only works because it repeats. On Mondays and Wednesdays my son has soccer after school, so I leave the office early on those days. My daughter has piano once a week, on Thursdays, and my wife takes her. Every other Friday we have pizza night, and the kids choose the movie, which means we usually watch the same three movies. Once a month we drive to my parents' house for Sunday lunch. That is the normal schedule. Do we stick to it? Most weeks, yes. Now and then something breaks. A meeting runs late, or somebody forgets the soccer bag at home, and then we change one thing, not everything. The rule in our house is simple: we can move a day, but we never cancel pizza night.
